paper.title: How simple can you go? An off-the-shelf transformer approach to molecular dynamics
paper.file_name: 32_How simple can you go - An off-the-shelf transformer approach to molecular dynamics.pdf
paper.research_summary: This paper presents MD-ET, an edge transformer adapted for molecular dynamics with minimal physical inductive biases (no built-in rotational equivariance or energy conservation), trained on the QCML dataset. It evaluates performance on benchmarks (QCML, MD17, Ko2020, xxMD, SPICE), analyzes approximate equivariance and energy conservation, and assesses stability and faithfulness of NVE and NVT simulations.

tasks.task_name_raw: molecular dynamics simulation using machine learning force fields
tasks.objective: Develop and evaluate a minimally biased neural network model for predicting atomic forces to enable stable and faithful molecular dynamics simulations.
constraints: off-the-shelf transformer architecture with minimal modification
output_goal: stable NVE and NVT molecular dynamics trajectories

evidence.text: We present a recipe for MD using an edge transformer (ET), an “off-the-shelf” transformer architecture that has been minimally modified for the MD domain, termed MD-ET. Our model implements neither built-in equivariance nor energy conservation.

We thus study an extreme case: we present and evaluate the best MD model we can build using a minimal amount of MD-specific design features. Specifically, we aim to use an architecture that could be used in some related ML setting with minimal changes.

stages.stage_goal: Obtain a large-scale quantum chemistry reference dataset spanning the periodic table, including out-of-equilibrium structures and different spin and charge states.

evidence.text: We modify an edge transformer (ET)43,44 with MD-specific embedding layers and train on the new QCML database.45 QCML ranges across the periodic table, including out-of-equilibrium structures and different spin and charge states, and includes properties for a subset of ∼30 × 106 entries calculated with density functional theory accuracy at the PBE0 level46,47 (including dispersion corrections48,49).

stages.stage_goal: Create train/validation/test splits ensuring conformational integrity and apply random rotations and reflections to learn approximate O(3)-equivariance.

evidence.text: We create an approximate 90%/5%/5% split from QCML. As QCML contains multiple conformations for each structure sampled along its normal modes, we ensure that all conformations of a structure are assigned to the same split. To learn approximate equivariance, we use data augmentation: during pretraining, we duplicate each batch once and apply random rotations and reflections to both copies to form an augmented batch.

stages.stage_goal: Train the MD-ET model to predict atomic forces directly (not via energy gradient) on the QCML dataset.

evidence.text: Instead of predicting a combined loss50 of energies and forces or calculating forces as the negative gradient of the predicted energy with respect to positions, we predict forces directly.

stages.stage_name_raw: benchmark evaluation on force prediction accuracy
stages.stage_goal: Assess the mean absolute error (MAE) of predicted atomic forces against ground truth on standard datasets (QCML, MD17, Ko2020, xxMD, SPICE).

evidence.text: In Table I, we present the mean absolute error (MAE) of force predictions for MD-ET, SpookyNet,70 and PaiNN21 on the QCML evaluation set at the end of pretraining.

Table IV compares the force root mean squared errors (RMSE) of MD-ET with a 4th-generation Behler–Parinello neural network, 4G-BPNN (high-dimensional neural network potential, 4G-HDNNP),67 and SpookyNet70 on selected systems from the Ko2020 dataset.

stages.stage_name_raw: evaluation of MD simulation stability and faithfulness
stages.stage_goal: Run NVE and NVT molecular dynamics simulations and measure stability (time until instability), faithfulness (h(r) score), and observables (velocity autocorrelation spectra).

evidence.text: Stability is measured by the time until a simulation becomes unstable (capped at 300 ps), and faithfulness is measured by h(r), the distribution of interatomic distances.74

To evaluate the degree to which MD-ET produces faithful MD simulations, we run 1 ns NVT simulations using the stochastic velocity rescaling (SVR or Bussi) thermostat... We then produce velocity–velocity autocorrelation spectra from these trajectories.

stages.stage_name_raw: analysis of equivariance and energy conservation
stages.stage_goal: Quantify the model's approximate rotational equivariance (via equivariance error Eeq) and approximate energy conservation (via Jacobian antisymmetry ratio λ and NVE energy drift).

evidence.text: Bigi et al.29 examine the Jacobian matrix of the force prediction with respect to atom positions J ∈R3n×3n to quantify energy conservation. The Jacobian of a perfectly energy-conserving prediction should be a symmetric matrix since it is the Hessian of the molecular energy.

We modify an edge transformer (ET)43,44 with MD-specific embedding layers and train on the new QCML database.45 QCML ranges across the periodic table, including out-of-equilibrium structures and different spin and charge states, and includes properties for a subset of ∼30 × 106 entries calculated with density functional theory accuracy at the PBE0 level46,47 (including dispersion corrections48,49).

We perform supervised pretraining on the new QCML dataset.45
In Table I, we present the mean absolute error (MAE) of force predictions for MD-ET, SpookyNet,70 and PaiNN21 on the QCML evaluation set at the end of pretraining.
We also report results for training the model directly on MD17. Since there is some overlap with the pretraining set, fine-tuning results for ethanol (marked with a ∗) have only limited significance.

The MD17 dataset15 consists of MD trajectories for small organic molecules and has been proposed as a benchmark by Fu et al.74 Models are evaluated not only for their prediction accuracy (MAE) but also for their simulation stability and faithfulness.

Table II compares MD-ET with several state-of-the-art models. In addition to fine-tuning ET-MD for 2000 steps, which we see as the default way to use a large-scale pretrained model, we also report results for training the model directly on MD17.

Table IV compares the force root mean squared errors (RMSE) of MD-ET with a 4th-generation Behler–Parinello neural network, 4G-BPNN (high-dimensional neural network potential, 4G-HDNNP),67 and SpookyNet70 on selected systems from the Ko2020 dataset.

The xxMD dataset by Pengmei et al.68 goes beyond the MD17 dataset by incorporating nonadiabatic MD trajectories specifically designed to capture chemical reactions, including geometries sampled from the PES of reactive intermediates, transition states, and products.

All previously evaluated datasets contain conformers of a single, relatively small structure (∼10-20 atoms). The SPICE dataset contains several subsets with conformers of multiple structures with a size of up to 96 atoms.69
